sections.title: What is Tae Kwon-Do
sections.summary: Tae Kwon-Do is a Korean unarmed combat art for self-defence that also serves as a disciplined way of life.

items.title: The name
items.text: The name joins words for jumping and kicking with the foot, striking or smashing with the hand, and the idea of a way or art.

items.title: Self-defence
items.text: Students learn to defend through strikes, kicks, blocks, evasion and interception.

items.title: Way of life
items.text: It is also a discipline that shapes character, and used carelessly it can be dangerous.

sections.title: History
sections.summary: The art grew out of older Oriental fighting traditions and was refined into its modern form in Korea.

items.text: The source page gives only a brief overview: Tae Kwon-Do descends from ancient Oriental combat methods and was perfected in Korea.

sections.title: The Tenets
sections.summary: Five guiding principles that every student works to live by, in and out of the dojang.

items.title: Courtesy
items.text: Be polite and respectful to instructors, seniors and fellow students.

items.title: Integrity
items.text: Be honest with yourself and know right from wrong.

items.title: Perseverance
items.text: Keep working towards a goal, whether a new grade or a technique.

items.title: Self Control
items.text: Stay calm and never lose your temper; train within your own ability.

items.title: Indomitable Spirit
items.text: Show courage and stand by your principles even against overwhelming odds.

sections.title: Student Oath
sections.summary: Five promises each student makes about conduct and the responsible use of the art.

items.text: I will follow the rules and regulations of the Association.
I will work to remain modest.
I will be courteous and respectful to all members, especially seniors.
I will use the art only to defend myself or to protect those who cannot.
I will never misuse what I have learned.

sections.title: Conduct in the Dojang
sections.summary: A set of bows and greetings marks arriving, training and leaving.

items.text: Bow as you enter the dojang.
Bow to the instructor from a respectful distance.
Greet your fellow students.
Bow to the instructor when lining up at the start of class.
Bow to the instructor when lining up at the end of class.
Bow again as you leave.

sections.title: Being a Good Student
sections.summary: Ten points on attitude, loyalty, example and reliability.

items.text: Stay keen to learn and ask questions; you can learn anywhere.
Give more than your fees: help with demonstrations, teaching and dojang tasks.
Set a good example for lower grades.
Be loyal and do not criticise your instructor, the art or its teaching methods.
Practise and try to apply what your instructor teaches.
Remember your behaviour outside the dojang reflects on the art and your instructor.
If your instructor disapproves of a technique learned elsewhere, drop it or train where you learned it.
Never be disrespectful; if you disagree, follow the instruction first and discuss it afterwards.
Arrive early and attend regularly.
Never betray a trust.

sections.title: Rules & Regulations
sections.summary: Fifteen practical rules covering membership, fees, dress, behaviour and grading.

items.text: Complete and sign the required forms before you begin training.
Obtain TAGB membership and a record card after your first four weeks.
Pay fees in the first week of each month; late payment carries a penalty.
Do not let fee arrears build up.
Give one month's notice to adjust fees for breaks such as holidays.
If you miss lessons and fees for two months or more, pay a re-enrolment fee before returning.
No smoking, eating, drinking or jewellery in the dojang.
Never smoke while wearing a dobok.
Take your belt off when eating or drinking in your dobok.
After your first grading, train in a dobok unless the instructor allows tracksuit or street clothes.
The most senior student present starts training until the instructor arrives.
Misusing the art leads to disciplinary action.
Grading depends on attendance, the instructor's judgement and technical ability.
To change schools you need a transfer form and prior permission from both instructors.
Own a Students Handbook after your first grading.

sections.title: Why Patterns (Tul)
sections.summary: Patterns are set sequences of attacks and defences against imaginary opponents, used to measure progress and sharpen technique.

items.title: What a pattern is
items.text: A fixed series of mostly defensive and offensive movements performed against one or more imaginary opponents; it shows a student's progress and skill.

items.title: Benefits
items.text: Patterns refine technique, help sparring, improve flexibility and freedom of movement, teach body shifting, build muscle, balance and breath control, and teach things other training does not.

items.title: Why twenty-four
items.text: General Choi Hong Hi compared a human life to one day; the twenty-four patterns stand for the twenty-four hours of a day, or his whole life, and a lasting legacy for mankind.

items.title: Performing patterns
items.text: Start and finish on the same spot; keep correct posture and facing; tense and relax at the right moments; move rhythmically without stiffness; follow the speed changes; perfect each pattern before the next; understand each movement's purpose; make every movement realistic.
